reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a PancakeSwap front-running bot with claims of tenfold returns and up to 100 BNB per day, then directs viewers to deploy, fund, and activate a contract. It claims automated trades will return 90% to the viewer's wallet while retaining 10% in the protocol, though it warns that fees may exceed some gains and the stated returns and contract behavior are unverified.

follow the description of the video as far as downloading Metamask. And also funding it. Make sure that it's connected to the Binance Smart Chain
the next step in this process is just funding your contract, which is pretty simple
I'm just going to do 0.5 BNB. Actually might just make it one.
the transaction is confirmed, so it was sent to the contract.

opening.argument: The presentation includes a concrete risk qualification rather than an unconditional promise. It warns that inadequate funding or high burn fees can make the contract lose more in fees than it earns, and recommends more capital only to cover those possible costs. That is materially different from representing every outcome as guaranteed. The speaker also describes the result as personal experience and says transaction reports could be shown, leaving room for verification rather than asking viewers to accept a guaranteed return.

citations.quote: the contract will basically waste in fees more than make profit.
I recommend funding the contract with around 1 - 0.5 BNB just to make sure that won't happen.
I've had really good luck with this in the last few weeks. I've made several hundred BNB, which I can show the transaction reports on BSCscan to. Corroborate that.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account emphasizes the title's promotional claim and the funding steps, but it omits the explicit warning that fees can exceed profit. The title alone does not establish that the speaker guaranteed the result, and a recommendation to account for burn and gas fees is a qualification, not proof of deception.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A warning about fees does not withdraw the central earnings pitch. The speaker still says the process automatically buys and sells, returns 90% of profit, and can reach a very large daily amount. Those statements present an unusually favorable outcome while the supplied material does not independently establish that the claimed returns occurred.

you can have upwards of 100 BNB a day if. You use a larger amount than what I started with.

opening.argument: The content is structured as a technical walkthrough of Solidity and Remix operations. It explains creating a contract file, copying contract information, selecting the compiler version, deploying through injected Web3, and checking the resulting address. Those are observable programming and blockchain-tool procedures. The speaker's account is presented as a demonstration of how the software is supposed to operate, including its interaction with PancakeSwap, rather than as proof that viewers will receive a fixed return.

We're gonna do injected web 3.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The presence of operational instructions does not convert a technical demonstration into a deceptive offer. The opposing account treats every deployment step as solicitation, but the same sequence is also what a viewer would need to reproduce and inspect the stated tool behavior. The material's technical focus remains clear.

citations.quote: you can pause this video if you need time right now.
So we should get a trans- yeah, we should get a transaction confirmation here, right.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it a tutorial does not make the demonstrated outcome merely educational. The walkthrough explicitly tells viewers to fund the deployed contract and then press its action control; it describes those operations as the route to automated buying, selling, and wallet returns. The technical format therefore supports the promotion rather than neutralizing it.

we'll just go over here and press. The action button.
It will automatically sell within one minute

opening.argument: What is shown is a software workflow using ordinary wallets, a development environment, a blockchain network, and a decentralized exchange. The supplied material does not ask viewers for a password, seed phrase, or direct payment to the presenter; it describes connecting a wallet and sending funds to a contract address. Nor does it establish a downline, recruitment scheme, or paid membership. On this record, the content can be understood as explaining a blockchain service and its stated operation, while the actual profitability remains something a viewer would need to assess independently.

Make sure that it's connected to the Binance Smart Chain
we're just going to send some funds to that contract that we just created.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account labels the contract funding as inherently disqualifying, but funding a contract is part of the described blockchain operation and is not the same as requesting account credentials or recruiting others. The record also includes a contract address and a visible transaction workflow, which is consistent with an ordinary on-chain service demonstration.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing credential request is beside the point: the core concern is that viewers are instructed to place BNB into a contract and activate it for promised profit. The material itself ties that deposit to front-running and says returns are sent back to the wallet, so this is more than a neutral description of software tools.
